newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - Belgium safely on track for EMU, says PM Dehaene.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Belgium safely on track for EMU, says PM Dehaene.

text.p: Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene said on Tuesday revisions to the 1997 budget agreed last weekend guaranteed Belgium a place in a single European currency from the start.

"The 1997 budget is of vital importance for our country because it will be part of our entry exam to (European economic and monetary union), which will be taken at the start of 1998," Dehaene said in a speech to parliament to present the outcome of the annual spring budget review.

"These revisions to the 1997 budget have made it possible to limit the budget deficit of all public authorities to 2.9 percent (of gross domestic product) which will allow our country to take part in EMU from the start," Dehaene added.
The 1996 deficit stood at 3.4 percent of GDP.

The 10.2 billion franc ($292 million) austerity package, details of which were released on Monday, mainly hits the corporate world. Belgian utility company Electrabel NV will have to pay an extra 1.5 billion franc tax on earnings while an extra tax on turnover of pharmaceutical companies will raise 1.8 billion francs in 1997.
Business people will also be hit by the obligation for non-managing partners in private companies to start paying withholding taxes on their income, which will raise 1.2 billion.
A crackdown on evasion of value added taxes is expected to bring in an extra two billion francs, while spending cuts at several ministries will save a total of three billion francs.
Dehaene said the new austerity measures represented only 0.1 percent of GDP, much less than has been required in neighbouring countries to keep on track for EMU.
"It is a certainty that Belgium is able to meet the convergence requirements of the Maastricht Treaty because the budget rests on a triple safety margin," Dehaene added.

First, Dehaene said, the deficit target at 2.9 percent was below the 3.0 percent norm permitted in the Maastricht Treaty. Secondly, the 1997 growth forecast was unchanged at 2.1 percent, compared with an average 2.9 percent of recent forecasts. Thirdly, there is a 20 billion franc safety margin designed to counter possible adverse developments on financial markets.

Budget Minister Herman Van Rompuy said the 20 billion franc margin meant that the 2.9 percent target would be hit even if short-term interest rates rose by 300 basis points above their current level of 3.60 percent.
Dehaene added the fight against unemployment would be the focus of the second half of the government's four-year term in office, which began in May 1995.
Dehaene said that before its summer recess, the government would organise five special cabinet meetings, each focusing on single issue problems.

The five issues were: job creation and small and medium-sized companies; information and telecommunication technologies; the functioning of the civil service; improving democracy on the basis of recommendations of an all-party parliamentary working group; and the fight against poverty and social exclusion.
